prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery-first case in the sense I care about: a 2011 theoretical prediction that a specific, simple geometric knob (the twist angle) quenches the kinetic energy, followed by the 2018 experiments in which nature actually delivered correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Theory made a sharp, falsifiable statement and the laboratory confirmed it, which is the opposite of elegant theory waiting for clues. It created a field that has spread across van der Waals materials, and it has been reproduced by many independent groups. Having listened to colleagues I now put this first. It is the entry with the broadest support (seven of eight openings rank it), and the support comes from members who weigh it from very different fields, including the experimentalists who note that the basic phase diagram is reproducible. Most importantly, it has a clean theory-plus-experiment attribution that fits within three names, which my own first choice, IceCube, does not do convincingly.
statement.case_against: The microscopic pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still not settled, and sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder make some claims soft; a prize in which the headline phase is not understood may later look hasty. There are also genuine attribution problems that the supplied trio does not resolve: earlier flat-band work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and the co-first experimental authors (Cao, Fatemi and colleagues) are outside the credited names, and Cory Dean's group made closely related contributions. If the committee decides that the credit cannot be drawn defensibly, the prize would be better postponed or moved to a field where the allocation is cleaner.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts the Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero pairing as sensible but flags the earlier flat-band identification by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, the experimental co-authors Cao and Fatemi, and the possibility that a more stable moire result (the fractional Chern insulator) should wait for later.
responses.response: I take the attribution caveat seriously, and I agree the earlier Lopes dos Santos work is a real complication. But the decisive and quantitative statement that the lowest bands become flat at a small discrete set of angles is the continuum-model calculation of 2011, and the discovery that made the world pay attention is the 2018 experiment. A citation phrased around the prediction of the magic angle and the discovery of the correlated and superconducting states describes exactly that, and does not claim the earliest observation that bands flatten. I would not wait for the fractional Chern insulator: it is a downstream consequence of the platform that this prize would open, not an alternative to it, and waiting risks losing the chance to credit the founders while the field is still young.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for the theory-before-experiment link and large impact on quantum materials, while asking whether the third credited name is really needed for a fair configuration.
responses.response: I share the theory-before-experiment appeal. On the third name, I would keep all three. Bistritzer and MacDonald are the two authors of the prediction, and a prize that credited only one of them would arbitrarily split a single paper. Dropping Bistritzer to leave a theory-experiment pair would be the simplest fix, but it would be unfair to the person who did the computation. Since the limit is three, this is the configuration with the most defensible credit. If you or Olsson think the allocation among the experimental team is a problem, I would still prefer to say so openly than to change the theory side.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube second and gets to a single-laureate option for Halzen, but concedes that one name may under-represent the early experimental leadership and the wider collaboration, and that source identification is still modest.
responses.response: This is where you and I started with the same view and where I now move. I put IceCube first because it is a new window onto the universe, learned from nature, with a century-old cosmic-ray question behind it. Your own caveat is the strongest argument against my opening ranking: a Halzen-only prize rests on one person for a detector built by many, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND ancestors not in the credit, and the source identification (the single TXS 0506+056 coincidence, the Galactic plane map) is still statistical. The astrophysics is right for a prize, but the credit and the maturity are not yet. I keep it as an alternative, and I would revisit it if the committee can find a defensible second and third name.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical lattice clocks first as a clean controllable quantum experiment at the 1e-18 level, with Katori and Ye as a defensible pair, while asking whether it is an incremental extension of the earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
responses.response: I respect this case, and the attribution (Katori's magic-wavelength concept, Ye's record performance) is cleaner than for most candidates. My reservation is about the nature of the discovery rather than the quality. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems already cover the principal conceptual ground of laser-based frequency metrology, and what lattice clocks add is a large improvement in precision and a promise of tests of relativity and constants that have not yet turned up anything. That is great measurement science, but I do not yet see a result from nature that changes how we think. If a redefinition of the second or a first anomalous result comes, I would rank it much higher. I keep it as a serious alternative because three of you rank it first and I may be undervaluing the instrument.

uncertainties: Whether the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene needs to be better understood before the prize is justified, or whether the discovery of the states is enough.
How the committee should treat Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto and the co-first experimental authors, who are not in the supplied credited names.
Whether the optical lattice clock candidate is judged a new discovery or an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I am relying on memory and have not verified priority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) are in high-energy theory and do not touch any shortlisted candidate. My interest in gravity bears on the nanohertz background, B029, which I do not propose.
